input:
In this tutorial passage, we will explore the important distinction between absolute error and relative error, using a pressure measurement as our worked example. Suppose that we have a pressure reading of 331 units, and suppose that the tolerance associated with this reading is 2% of the reading itself. On this basis, the absolute error works out at 6.62 units, and it is this figure that tells us how far the reading might actually lie from the true value in the units of the measurement.

The absolute error is expressed in the same units as the measurement, which makes it directly interpretable: an absolute error of 6.62 units on a reading of 331 units means that the true value is expected to lie within that distance on either side of the reading. The relative error, by contrast, expresses the error as a proportion of the reading, and in this case it is simply the tolerance of 2% restated in relative form. Relative error is particularly useful when measurements of very different sizes need to be compared on a like-for-like basis.

It is also important to note that error should not be confused with uncertainty, even though the two terms are often used interchangeably in everyday language. Error refers to the difference between a reading and the true value, whereas uncertainty describes the range within which the true value is believed to lie. Keeping these two concepts clearly separate is essential for sound measurement practice.
target:
A pressure reading of 331 units with a tolerance of 2% of reading carries an absolute error of 6.62 units. The tutorial separates the two forms of the same statement: absolute error, stated in the units of the measurement, and relative error, stated as a fraction of the reading.

Absolute error is the difference between the reading and the true value, expressed in the units of the measurement itself. It answers the question the operator asks: how far, in units, might this reading lie from the value it reports? Relative error divides the absolute error by the reading, so the same instrument performance can be compared between a small reading and a large one. The conversion in this example is a single step: 2% of 331 units is 6.62 units, obtained by multiplying the reading by the tolerance fraction. The tolerance is quoted as a percentage of reading, not of full scale, and the basis matters: a percentage of full scale would give a different absolute error at the same reading, and a larger one wherever the reading sits below full scale.

Error is not uncertainty. Error is the difference between a reading and the true value; it has a sign in principle, even where the sign is unknown. Uncertainty is the range within which the true value is believed to lie, and it is the quantity a measurement report can actually state. A reading can therefore be reported with its uncertainty, but never with its error, because the true value that defines the error is the thing the measurement is trying to find.
